title: Quality Assurance that Works! Education Salles, Dominic
author: Salles, Dominic
summary: Dominic Salles responds to a Mark Enser post on school quality assurance by proposing a more structured alternative based on his experience leading school improvement. The central argument is that quality assurance too often becomes an exercise in reassurance rather than understanding -- learning walks drift toward surface features, book looks confirm compliance rather than growth, and data stands in for professional judgment -- because it is disconnected from a clear definition of what leaders actually need to know. Salles' preferred alternative is a precise checklist structure: not ambiguous criteria open to subjective interpretation, but specific, universal teaching behaviors that are known to produce learning gains, applied consistently across all subjects. He distinguishes between proxies for teaching and the actual goal (learning), arguing that a small set of well-chosen universal teaching routines -- his school used 'The Essential 8' -- creates conditions for subject leaders, coaches, and teachers to improve in a measurable, cumulative way. The article delivers four concrete checklists covering curriculum quality, lesson visits, book looks, and personal CPD cycles, each grounded in the principle that precision and focus are more powerful than rich but ambiguous frameworks.
points: * The kiss of death for school improvement is over-nuanced frameworks: when QA criteria become wide, interpretable, and hedged with qualification, they lose the precision that makes them actionable -- a small number of clear, universal behaviors everyone is expected to develop is more powerful than a rich but ambiguous rubric. * Learning is three wheels back from the teacher: curriculum is the first wheel, and a strong curriculum with an average teacher produces more progress than a brilliant teacher working from a weak one -- QA systems focused heavily on teaching style while neglecting curriculum are measuring the wrong variable. * Team book looks -- where teachers judge their own books directly alongside the most successful colleagues in the same department -- are more developmentally powerful than isolated marking reviews because they make differences in quality visible and attributable. * Personal CPD effectiveness depends on the teacher choosing 2-3 specific things to work on within a 13-week block, measuring their impact, and writing a 60-day plan at the end -- continuous amorphous 'professional development' without this measurement loop rarely produces transferable skill. * The QA checklist must be specific enough that a leader doing a lesson visit can count measurable things (students on task, visualiser use, routines executed) rather than making holistic impressionistic judgments -- the KPI structure gives the leader a basis for honest conversation rather than vague praise or criticism. quotes: Effective quality assurance begins with a simple question: what do we need to know in order to improve teaching in this school?

A common problem is that quality assurance becomes an exercise in reassurance rather than understanding. Activities are chosen because they feel familiar or visible, not because they tell leaders something meaningful about learning.
We focused on them because they were 'proxies for learning'. Not teaching. Teaching is simply a proxy for learning. Learning is the end goal.

A student diligently using Sparx Maths would learn way more than a student in the class of a bottom 30% teacher. Probably even an average teacher. An average teacher teaching a brilliant curriculum will get way more progress than a brilliant teacher teaching a fluffy curriculum.
This is the kiss of death for school improvement and quality assurance. Instead, you want to be precise. You want to focus only on what matters most. Nuance is for the other stuff.
Do you do these together as a team, so everyone judges their own books in comparison to the most successful teachers?

What has the teacher chosen to work on in this 13 week block? They will choose from: Their reflections on Book Looks; The results of their assessments and public exams; Student voice; Lesson Visits; Research (desirable, but not required)." Page 2
